paragraphs.title: A Universal Call to Praise God

easy.explanation: Verse 1 says, “Make a joyful noise unto God, all ye lands.”
easy.q: Who is called to make a joyful noise unto God?

easy.explanation: Verse 2 commands, “Sing forth the honour of his name.”
Verse 4 says, “All the earth shall worship thee, and shall sing unto thee.”
easy.q: What shall all the earth do before God?

answers: Making a joyful noise, singing, praising, and worshipping
Fighting, fleeing, hiding, and remaining silent
Building an altar, fasting, sleeping, and mourning
medium.explanation: The verses call the earth to shout, sing, praise, and worship God.
medium.q: Which sequence of actions appears in verses 1–4?

answers: Because His works are terrible and His power causes His enemies to submit
Because He needs help from the nations
Because He wants the nations to leave the earth
medium.explanation: Verse 3 praises God’s terrible works and great power before which His enemies submit.
medium.q: Why are the nations called to recognize God’s works?

answers: God’s works are small and unimportant
God’s works are fearful, mighty, and awe-inspiring
God’s works are hidden and unknown
medium.explanation: “Terrible” in this verse expresses awe at God’s mighty and fearful works.
medium.q: What does “How terrible art thou in thy works!” mean in context?

answers: It is limited to one family
It extends to every land and people
It is addressed only to rulers
challenge.explanation: The phrase presents praise as a universal call to all lands.
challenge.q: What does the phrase “all ye lands” show about the scope of the call to praise?

answers: Singing is a way to glorify and honor His name
challenge.explanation: The psalm joins singing with making God’s praise glorious.
challenge.q: How is singing connected with honoring God’s name?

answers: His enemies become stronger than He is
His enemies ignore His power completely
His enemies submit themselves because of His power
challenge.explanation: Verse 3 says that through the greatness of God’s power His enemies submit themselves unto Him.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between God’s great power and His enemies?

paragraphs.title: God’s Deeds and Rule over the Nations

answers: Come and see the works of God
easy.explanation: Verse 5 says, “Come and see the works of God.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist invite people to do?

answers: He turned it into dry land
He hid it from the nations
easy.explanation: Verse 6 says, “He turned the sea into dry land.”
easy.q: What did God do to the sea?

easy.explanation: Verse 7 says, “his eyes behold the nations.”

answers: The crossing displays God’s works and leads to rejoicing in Him
The crossing prevents the psalmist from rejoicing
The crossing is described as the work of the enemies
medium.explanation: After describing the crossing on foot, the psalm says, “there did we rejoice in him.”
medium.q: How does the crossing of the sea relate to the psalmist’s joy?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to the mighty things God has done.
medium.q: What does “the works of God” mean in this passage?

answers: Everlasting and directed toward the nations
medium.explanation: Verse 7 says that God rules by His power forever and beholds the nations.
medium.q: How are God’s rule and watchfulness described?

answers: God acts openly and watches over the peoples
God works only in one place
God has no concern for the nations
challenge.explanation: The passage presents God as both active in history and watchful over the nations.
challenge.q: What idea connects the invitation to see God’s works with the statement that His eyes behold the nations?

answers: God leads His people through different obstacles
The waters are places of rest
The waters represent only the enemies
challenge.explanation: The two water images emphasize God’s ability to provide a way through difficulties.
challenge.q: What does the mention of the sea and the flood together suggest?

answers: The rebellious may boast without limit
The rebellious must not lift themselves up against God’s rule
challenge.explanation: The verse warns rebellious people not to exalt themselves before God’s everlasting authority.
challenge.q: What warning is contained in “let not the rebellious exalt themselves”?

easy.explanation: Verse 8 says, “O bless our God, ye people.”
easy.q: Who is called to bless God?

easy.explanation: Verse 9 says that God “suffereth not our feet to be moved.”
easy.q: What did God not allow the feet of His people to do?

easy.explanation: Verse 12 ends, “but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place.”
easy.q: Where did God bring His people after fire and water?

answers: Preservation, testing and affliction, followed by deliverance
Turning away from God and prayer
medium.explanation: The passage describes God preserving life, testing His people, allowing affliction, and finally bringing them into relief.
medium.q: What process is described in verses 8–12?

answers: Because He preserved their souls and brought them through trouble
medium.explanation: God held their soul in life and brought them safely through their trials.
medium.q: Why should the people bless God according to this passage?

medium.explanation: The next phrase compares God’s testing to silver being tried.
medium.q: What does “thou hast proved us” mean?

answers: Testing can examine and refine a person
Silver is the purpose of the psalm
challenge.explanation: The image of tried silver presents suffering as a process of examination and refinement.
challenge.q: What does the comparison with silver being tried emphasize?

answers: They show movement from danger and distress to relief
They describe two kinds of celebration
They cancel the idea of deliverance
challenge.explanation: Fire and water represent severe trials, while the wealthy place represents deliverance and relief.
challenge.q: How do “fire and water” and “a wealthy place” work together in the passage?

answers: One describes the enemies and the other describes a sacrifice
challenge.explanation: Both statements emphasize that God preserved life and kept His people from falling.
challenge.q: What connection exists between God holding the soul in life and not allowing the feet to be moved?

answers: Into the house of his enemies
easy.explanation: Verse 13 says, “I will go into thy house with burnt offerings.”
easy.q: Where does the psalmist promise to go?

easy.explanation: He says, “I will pay thee my vows.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist promise to pay?

easy.explanation: Verse 15 lists burnt sacrifices of fatlings, the incense of rams, bullocks, and goats.
easy.q: Which offerings does the psalmist mention?

medium.explanation: Verse 14 says his mouth spoke the vows “when I was in trouble.”
medium.q: When had the psalmist spoken the vows he now promises to pay?

answers: The offerings express thanksgiving and fulfill a promise
The offerings show opposition to God
medium.explanation: After deliverance, the psalmist comes to God’s house to fulfill his vows with offerings.
medium.q: What is the relationship between deliverance and the offerings?

medium.explanation: The KJV word “goats” refers to the animals included with the bullocks and other sacrifices.
medium.q: What are “goats” in the list of offerings?

answers: The vows were spoken in trouble and the offerings followed deliverance
The offerings came before every prayer
The vows had no connection with trouble
challenge.explanation: The psalmist recalls trouble, the vows spoken then, and their fulfillment afterward.
challenge.q: What does the order of trouble, vows, and offerings reveal?

answers: The psalmist intends to express generous thanksgiving
challenge.explanation: The many offerings show a serious and generous response of gratitude.
challenge.q: What may be inferred from the variety and abundance of offerings?

answers: It describes promises spoken earlier that will now be fulfilled
It removes the need for offerings
challenge.explanation: The psalmist’s spoken vows are the promises he now intends to pay.
challenge.q: How does “my lips have uttered” connect with the rest of the passage?

paragraphs.title: Personal Testimony and an Answered Prayer

answers: Only the kings of the nations
easy.explanation: Verse 16 says, “Come and hear, all ye that fear God.”
easy.q: Whom does the psalmist invite to hear his testimony?

easy.explanation: Verse 17 says, “I cried unto him with my mouth.”
easy.q: To whom did the psalmist cry?

answers: He heard and attended to it
easy.explanation: Verses 19–20 say that God heard the prayer and attended to its voice.
easy.q: What did God do with the psalmist’s prayer?

answers: What God did for his soul
The building of a new city
medium.explanation: He says, “I will declare what he hath done for my soul.”
medium.q: What does the psalmist want to declare to those who fear God?

answers: He must not regard iniquity in his heart
He must never call upon God
medium.explanation: Verse 18 says that if he regarded iniquity in his heart, the Lord would not hear him.
medium.q: What condition does the psalmist mention concerning his prayer?

answers: With blessing for God, who heard the prayer and did not remove His mercy
medium.explanation: The final verse blesses God for hearing the prayer and not turning away His mercy.

answers: He presents freedom from cherished iniquity as related to God’s hearing
He says the heart has no connection with prayer
He says only sacrifices are heard
challenge.explanation: The psalmist says that regarding iniquity in his heart would prevent the Lord from hearing him.
challenge.q: What connection does the psalmist make between the heart and answered prayer?

answers: A movement from human prayer to God’s attentive response
A movement from praise to silence
A movement from prayer to sacrifice only
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from the psalmist’s cry to God’s hearing and attention.
challenge.q: What movement is shown from “I cried unto him” to “he hath attended”?

answers: He turns personal deliverance into testimony that encourages praise and thanksgiving
He hides God’s mercy from others
challenge.explanation: He invites God-fearing people to hear what God did for him and ends by blessing God.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the psalmist sharing his experience with those who fear God?
